plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to open Claude Code in a terminal, describe a small web app in plain English, get it built and running on your own computer, fix 3 common breakages by describing them, and save your work to GitHub so you can't lose it.
plan.horizon14: Later, around day 14: build a second small app from scratch and put it online where a friend can use it.
plan.horizon28: Later, around day 28: add sign-in and saved data to an app, and read enough of the code to spot when Claude went the wrong way.

picture.name: Hiring a contractor
picture.line: Claude Code is a skilled builder you've hired for your house; you don't swing the hammer, but you decide what gets built, you check the work, and you keep the keys.

chapters.title: Meet the builder: the terminal and your first request
chapters.covers: Install Claude Code, open it inside a folder (the terminal is a text window where you type commands instead of clicking), and ask it for one tiny thing you can see work.
chapters.outcome: You can start Claude Code in a folder, type a plain-English request, and see a file appear and run.
chapters.hook: Your first working program is about three sentences away, and none of them are code.

chapters.title: Writing a brief the builder can't misread
chapters.covers: How to describe what you want so Claude builds the right thing: the user, the one job, what it should look like when done, and what to leave out.
chapters.outcome: You can write a 5-line request that gets a working first version without going back and forth more than twice.
chapters.hook: Why 'make it better' is the worst instruction you can give a builder.

chapters.title: Walking the site: reading what got built
chapters.covers: The 4 kinds of files in a small web project (the page, the styling, the logic, the settings) and how to ask Claude to explain any of them in plain words.
chapters.outcome: You can open a project folder, name what each main file is for, and ask Claude to explain a piece you don't follow.
chapters.hook: A small web app is only 4 kinds of files. Which one does what?

chapters.title: When something breaks: describing the leak, not guessing the pipe
chapters.covers: How to copy an error message, tell Claude exactly what you did and what you saw, and check the fix yourself before moving on.
chapters.outcome: You can take an error from a red screen to a fixed and tested app by giving Claude the message and the steps that caused it.
chapters.hook: That red error message was written for Claude, not you. Hand it over.

chapters.title: Keeping the keys: saving every good version with Git and GitHub
chapters.covers: Git is a save-point system for code and GitHub is where those save points live online; you learn to commit (save), push (upload), and go back to a working version.
chapters.outcome: You can save a working version, upload it to GitHub, and restore yesterday's version when today's attempt goes wrong.
chapters.hook: One sentence brings back yesterday's working version, if you set this up first.

chapters.title: Work orders in small pieces: one feature at a time
chapters.covers: Why asking for one feature, testing it, and saving beats asking for 5 at once; and how to split a big idea into a numbered list of small jobs.
chapters.outcome: You can turn an app idea into 5 to 8 small jobs and build them one by one, with a saved version after each.
chapters.hook: Why one small job, tested and saved, beats five asked for at once.

chapters.title: Inspecting the work: the 3 checks before you trust a build
chapters.covers: How to test as a user, ask Claude to list what it changed and why, and keep your own notes file so the builder remembers your rules next session.
chapters.outcome: You can finish a session by testing the app, reading Claude's summary of changes, and writing the 3 to 5 rules you want followed next time.
chapters.hook: Claude forgets everything when you close the window, unless you leave it a note.
